content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a internal cluster validation index that is based on the notion of 'differential entropy' to assess the compactness and separability of a clustering solution. It relies on the assumptions i) that each cluster can be modeled using a Gaussian distribution and ii) that clusters centers also follow a Gaussian distribution.  The proposed index is compared to several alternatives using embeddings obtained from deep neural networks pretrained on image and text datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The paper is well-written and clearly explained.

Weaknesses
There is no significant technical contribution. Combining internal and external cluster separation is typical in most clustering quality indices.
Differential entropy depends on the determinant of the covariance matrix, a well-known measure of cluster variance. 
Gaussian assumption is made both for the data distribution inside a cluster and the distribution of cluster centers, which is actually too restrictive.
There is no sufficient intuitive justification on why the proposed index would perform better than existing ones.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The method is simple and lacks in terms of originality and novelty. 
The paper is clearly written and the results seem to be easily reproducible (although no code is provided).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper presents an internal cluster validation index that is based on the differential entropy of multidimensional normal distribution. 
Given a cluster i with data mean \mu_i and data covariance Σ_i its compactness is computed as the entropy of the normal distribution N(\mu_i, Σ_i). The dispersion among clusters is computed as the entropy of the set of cluster centers, assuming that they are Gaussian distributed.

Major concerns about the paper.
1) The Gaussian assumption is too restrictive.
2) Differential entropy is essentially the determinant of Σ, which is a well-known measure of cluster variance.  
3) Experiments focus on embeddings from pretrained deep networks. The method should be evaluated on synthetic datasets with clusters of various shapes and known ground truth. It should also be tested on typical low dimensional benchmark datasets (e.g. from the UCI repository).
4) There is no sufficient intuitive justification on why the proposed index would perform better than several existing ones also relying on separation and compactness.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
**Comment 4.1**. The Gaussian assumption is too restrictive.  
**Response 4.1**:   Although we assume data follows normal distribution, it turns out that this assumption won’t affect its performance in scenarios where the data is deeply represented. The reasons are as follows:    
 (1)	Existing works have proved that the distribution of the deep representation is close to the normal distribution [1][2]. Hence, our hypothesis is robust to data that can be represented by deep pre-trained models. We appreciate this comment and have further clarified and discussed this in the revision.   
 (2)	To verify the above inference, some datasets without deep representation are also tested in the revision, e.g., real-world datasets from UCI Machine Learning Repository. Henze-Zirkler normality test [3] indicates that UCI datasets don’t conform to the normal distribution and the experimental results (Appendix E) show that the advantage of using our proposed internal index is not obvious. Specifically, for 15 test cases in total, our IP index can return the optimal clustering results in 11 cases while other indices also report 11 cases.  Furthermore, we obtain the representation of text datasets by TF-IDF (Appendix F) and the experimental results  shows our index performs worse than other indices  which demonstrates that the normal distribution assumption is indeed restrictive in our work, but it won’t affect the usage of our method over the data after deep representation. Considering that deep representation is already widely used, we believe that our method is still very practical.  
[1] Lee K, Lee K, Lee H, et al. A simple unified framework for detecting out-of-distribution samples and adversarial attacks[J]. NIPS, 2018.  
[2] Daneshmand H, Joudaki A, Bach F. Batch normalization orthogonalizes representations in deep random networks[J]. NIPS, 2021.  
[3] Henze, N., & Zirkler, B. (1990). A class of invariant consistent tests for multivariate normality. Communications in Statistics-Theory and Methods.  

**Comment 4.2**. Differential entropy is essentially the determinant of Σ, which is a well-known measure of cluster variance.  
**Response 4.2**：Thanks for your comment. In fact, differential entropy depends not only on the determinant of the covariance matrix but also on the rank of the covariance matrix. As mentioned in Section 3 - Preliminaries, if the covariance matrix is not full rank, the rank of covariance matrix < d and the determinant of covariance matrix is degenerated as the pseudo-determinant. Although the determinant of Σ is a well-known measure, such as AIC and BIC, it is worth noting that our index also takes into account the rank of the covariance matrix. Further, as mentioned in Section 4.2 – theoretical analysis, our index not only takes into account the traditional internal clustering criteria, i.e. compactness and separation, but also capture what traditional information criterion based indices, such as AIC and BIC, want to measure.  
 
**Comment 4.3**. Experiments focus on embeddings from pretrained deep networks. The method should be evaluated on synthetic  datasets with clusters of various shapes and known ground truth. It should also be tested on typical low dimensional benchmark datasets (e.g. from the UCI repository).  
**Response 4.3**：Thanks for the comment. In fact, we also use five UCI datasets for our experiments. Details can be seen in Appendix E. Evaluation results show our index is either on par or slightly better than competing indices. 

**Comment 4.4**. There is no sufficient intuitive justification on why the proposed index would perform better than several existing ones also relying on separation and compactness.  
**Response 4.4**：Thanks for the comment. We use two examples to illustrate the defects of the current internal indices in introduction. Moreover, experimental results also show the significant superiority of our index.

content.title: Thanks for the response
content.comment: Thank you for the response and revised version. I have read the revised version, the reply and and the comments of the other reviewers and I will retain my original score. My main concern remains the same: I do not find significant novelty in the proposed approach which attempts to tackle a difficult and well-studied problem in a rather typical way: it makes Gaussian assumptions and exploits the determinant of the covariance matrix.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new measure for internal clustering evaluation. To compute this measure, one first computes the differential entropy for each cluster (assuming that the elements are sampled from a multivariate normal distribution) and then subtracts the differential entropy for the cluster centers from the average entropy of individual clusters. Experimental results on several datasets with known cluster labels show the advantages of the new measure over existing ones.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Experimental results show significant improvements on the considered datasets

Weaknesses:
- The assumption about the normal distribution is quite strong, and it is not clear how deviations from this assumption would affect the quality of the measure
- There is no theoretical or empirical analysis of the properties of the proposed measure

Detailed comments are below.

I am not very familiar with the literature on internal clustering evaluation measures, but there are works on theoretical analysis of such measures, for instance, papers discussing axioms desirable for these measures [1] or providing guarantees for convex clusters (Halkidi & Vazirgiannis, 2001). Then, an empirical evaluation was conducted by Liu et al. (2013), where the effect of noise, density, and shapes was analyzed. The current paper would benefit from more detailed related work where different approaches to comparing clustering measures are discussed.

Additionally, a more detailed analysis of the proposed measure would help to demonstrate its advantages. For instance, does this measure satisfy some desirable theoretical properties? Is it biased towards big or small clusters? (Such biases are formalized for external cluster evaluation measures, e.g., in [2].) How the measure performs for clusters with different levels of noise, different shapes, etc.? Such theoretical or empirical analysis can show the benefits and limitations of the proposed measure.

More details throughout the text can be helpful:
- The beginning of page 2: formalization of distance-based indices would help a reader to understand the motivating example.
- Formal definitions of the measures from Table 1 are needed to understand the existing measures and the differences between them and the proposed measure. (In Table 1, the intuition behind the measures is given.)
- More details on the information criterion are needed to understand the analogy at the beginning of page 6.
- Also, I could not get the main message of the paragraph “Effectiveness” in Section 4.2.
The detailed experimental setup can be moved to Appendix, which may give more space to explanations throughout the text.

Minor comments:
- Note that the differential entropy in equation (2) is for a one-dimensional case, while it is later used for d-dimensional vectors.
- To compute CP in equation (7), parameters of the multivariate normal have to be estimated, which needs to be mentioned in the text.
- The variable m (the number of samples in the k-th cluster) can be changed to reflect the dependency on k, e.g., m_k

Questions for the authors:
- Q1: The measure assumes that the elements within each cluster and cluster centers have multivariate normal distributions. In practice, this can be violated. What would happen in such cases? How sensitive is the measure to deviations from this assumption? Also, can we approximate the density and then approximate the integral (2) without this assumption?
- Q2: Could you please specify how accuracy is computed for clustering evaluation?

Some typos:
- “these implementation” (page 2, line 3)
- “the volume of two cluster vector space are the same” (page 2, line 8)
- “has also be used” (page 3, line 6)
- “the distance form the samples” (page 2, definition of I index)
- “are not good measure” (page 4)
- “ACC and ARI indicates” (page 6, line -7)
- “besults” (page 7, line -7)
- “CH obtain” (page 7, line -5)
- “Tabel” (page 7, line -5)
- Missing articles throughout the text

[1] Ben-David S., Ackerman M. Measures of clustering quality: A working set of axioms for clustering. NIPS 2008.

[2] Gösgens M., Tikhonov A., Prokhorenkova L. Systematic analysis of cluster similarity indices: How to validate validation measures. ICML 2021.

**Clarity** The paper is generally clearly written, but some background required for the understanding is not included.

**Novelty** To the best of my knowledge, the proposed measure is novel.

**Reproducibility** There are enough details to reproduce the experiments, but code is not provided.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an internal validation metric for model selection in clustering based on the average difference in differential entropy between each cluster and the cluster means when each cluster is treated as having a Gaussian distribution, as is the collection of cluster means.

Some experiments are included to show the practical performance in comparison with other internal metrics when data are clustered after being embedded with pre-trained neural networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Unfortunately I do not see any substantial strengths in the paper. Although there is some evidence of practical relevance, the experiments are a bit contrived and furthermore the implementation of some other metrics, such as AIC and BIC, is incorrect. First, AIC and BIC in their basic formulations should not be applied to the solution based on a hard mixture, such as k-means. Furthermore, if the authors would like to use these then it is sensible to use the same parameter estimates for them as in the proposed method since AIC and BIC are applicable for GMMs, which is the "assumption" underlying the proposed method.

Weaknesses:
- The authors argue that compactness metrics based on variance are flawed, and yet they propose one which is based solely on the differences between the volumes of the covariance matrices of the clusters and the between class covariance. It is not clear why their proposal is not similarly flawed.
- There does not seem to be any theoretical underpinning for the proposed approach, whereas if the "assumption" is that the data are from a Gaussian mixture then there are well motivated alternatives with sound theoretical underpinnings, such as AIC and BIC.
- The presentation and notation is unclear.
- The authors report the performance in terms of ACC and ARI, however other external validation metrics may tell a very different story.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity, both in terms of the writing, and in terms of the arguments put forward in support of the proposed method requires improvement. Without a theoretical justification, or at least a strong heuristic justification for the proposed metric, the proposal overall is not of a quality high enough for publication in a top tier conference such as ICLR. Regarding novelty, it is possible that the proposal is entirely new, however its similarity with likelihood based criteria (the negative entropy is directly connected to the expected log-likelihood) means that it is more tangential to existing methods than the authors seem to have noticed. In terms of reproducibility, I have concerns about the way in which existing metrics were implemented and without absolute clarity it is not certain that the results are reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, while there is arguably some evidence for practical relevance, the experiments are a bit too thin and potentially contrived to suit the proposed method, and there are questions regarding the correctness of the implementation of other metrics, to warrant acceptance in a top tier conference. Furthermore, even if there were no issues with the experiments, the lack of a sound justification (either theoretical, or at least a well argued heuristic) for the proposed method means that its performance in general is questionable.

UPDATE:

After considering the authors' responses to my and other reviewers' comments, as well as the reviewers' comments themselves, I do not see a reason to adjust my initial score/assessment of the paper.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
**Comment 2.1:** AIC and BIC in their basic formulations should not be applied to the solution based on a hard mixture, such as k-means.   
**Response 2.1:** Thanks for your comment. In fact, AIC and BIC can be applied to the solution based on a hard mixture. For example, Manning uses residual sum of squares or RSS in AIC to evaluate clustering results for K-means[1].  
[1] Manning, Christopher D. Introduction to information retrieval. Syngress Publishing,, 2008. Page 366.

**Comment 2.2:** The authors argue that compactness metrics based on variance are flawed, and yet they propose one which is based solely on the differences between the volumes of the covariance matrices of the clusters and the between class covariance. It is not clear why their proposal is not similarly flawed.   
**Response 2.2:**  In our paper, we have explained why our proposal can solve the drawbacks of previous variance based indices. For short, variance based compactness computation is misleading in some cases. As shown in Fig. 1(b) in introduction, we can easily observe that cluster B is more compact than cluster A. But the variances for both clusters are the same. In fact, covariance here is more suitable to measure the compactness, i.e., the covariances among pairs of variables in cluster A is smaller than that of cluster B. And our proposed index is motivated from the entropy perspective which theoretically measures the volumes of the cluster as stated in Section 4.2.

**Comment 2.3:** There does not seem to be any theoretical underpinning for the proposed approach, whereas if the "assumption" is that the data are from a Gaussian mixture then there are well motivated alternatives with sound theoretical underpinnings, such as AIC and BIC.  
**Response 2.3:** Thanks for your suggestion. As we mentioned in the Section 4.2 - Theoretical Analysis, our index is related to the generalized variance, which is proportional to the square of the volume generated by the d deviation vectors. Moreover, our index is similar to the information criterion. Hence, our index can also capture what traditional information criterion based indices want to measure, for example, AIC and BIC. In fact, we have already analyzed this in a theoretical way in Section 4.2.

**Comment 2.4.** The authors report the performance in terms of ACC and ARI, however other external validation metrics may tell a very different story.  
**Response 2.4:** Thanks for reminding us. We had added the third external validation metric, i.e., NMI, to evaluate the performance of our index in the revision. As stated in Section 5.2, our proposed IP index still greatly outperform other indices.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
AIC and BIC:
- The expressions RSS + 2*d*k for AIC and RSS + log(n)*d*k for BIC are fundamentally flawed and whether or not they have been used before should certainly not be propagated in literature. The obvious limitation is that the selection should not be dependent on the scale of the data. With these expressions I can always multiply the data by a large enough constant that I will always choose the number of clusters equal to the number of observations, and by a small enough constant that I will always select a single cluster. Furthermore, if the data have been scaled there are still issues with the internal cluster scale being smaller for larger number of clusters. A more appropriate formulation would be n*log(RSS) + 2*d*k for AIC and n*log(RSS) + log(n)*d*k for BIC as this is invariant to the scale of the data. However, this is still very problematic since the complexity of the model which includes cluster assignment is underestimated by d*k [1].

2.2
- I think the authors may have misunderstood my comment. I am using variance and covariance synonymously. Covariance captures compactness after rescaling according to the spectral properties of the covariance matrix. The naive spherical cluster model certainly is less flexible, but not necessarily less appropriate. Accepting the distinction between covariance and variance, the authors seem to have overlooked the fact that all likelihood based criteria for GMMs use the covariance, and indeed the volumne of the covariance matrices. So I still fail to see how their approach does not suffer the same "limitations" as AIC and BIC for a GMM. To reiterate my other point. Entropy and negative log-likelihood are equivalent in some contexts and so just saying that your metric is based on entropy does not strengthen the argument.

2.3
- With respect, I do not see 4.2 as a theoretical contribution nor a sound theoretical underpinning of the approach. This is just a description of what the proposed metric represents.

2.4
- Thank you for adding this. To reiterate, there is some evidence that the proposed approach works for the scenario you describe, however I still have doubts about the veracity of the experimental results without clarity on exactly how other metrics have been implemented and whether or not this has been done correctly, or at least appropriately.

I would like to finish with a comment about the general topic which the authors have chosen to address. I applaud the authors for identifying the importance of the problem, as this is, arguably, the "hardest" problem in clustering (determining the number of clusters, and the flexibility of each cluster when using additional hyperparameters). However, the literature is pregnant with heuristics for these selections, all of which work well sometimes and maybe fairly consistently across scenarios. However, to be able to develop something very impactful for publication in a top tier venue, I believe it is extremely unlikely unless there is a very strong theoretical argument or a very convincing heuristic justification for the new method. I do not mean to suggest that the proposal given by the authors is necessarily not a good one, only that the presentation currently given does not convey sufficiently why we can expect it to work well in general when compared with similar (e.g., other likelihood based criteria), and indeed very different metrics like those based on distance/nonparametrics.

[1] David P. Hofmeyr (2020), "Degrees of freedom and model selection for k-means clustering", Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 149, 106974

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a novel internal validation index for clustering, based on the differential entropy, named internal purity. The method is evaluated on different datasets, encoded with deep net representations, and compared with standard alternatives.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Positive points:
- The topic is definitely interesting
- The paper is well written and easy to read
- The structure of the manuscript is clear
- The experimental evaluation is rather extensive


Negative points:

1) the computation of the index can be problematic.
The method is based on the estimation of the differential entropy of the clusters. The estimation of the entropy is based on the assumption that data follows multivariate normal distribution, which I consider a rather strong and problematic assumption:

- In many clustering problems data are not normally distributed
- There can be problems in estimating covariance matrices in such high dimensional spaces
- Better alternatives exist: for example, you can consider alternative non parametric bypass entropy estimators. Actually different studies have been conducted on estimating Entropies without making any assumption on the shape (which may be not realistic) and without a direct estimation of the density (which may be very problematic in high dimensional spaces). A starting example can be the non parametric bypass entropy estimator of the Renyi entropy proposed in:

D. Pal, B. Poczos, and C. Szepesvari, “Estimation of Rényi entropy and mutual information based on generalized nearest-neighbor graphs,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 23, 2010, pp. 1849-1857.


2) Some comments on the experimental part.

- All the experiments are based on text-images which are pre-encoded with deep net representations. Is this crucial for the applied method? In other words, how well this method could generalize to non-deep representations? What about the application on original representations of non-image and non-text datasets?
Moreover, in the paper I did not find mention to the size of the embedding, which I guess is high (please report it in the paper). How does the method work in moderately dimensional datasets? I’m sure that other methods would increase their performances. 
Finally: while for representation recent state-of-the-art methods have been used, for clustering only classic approaches have been considered, such as K-means, Dbscan, GMM and HC. What if we use more recent and better performing methods? Moreover, most of these methods are returning convex clusters (i.e. somehow following Gaussianity). 

Without considering these three aspects it is difficult to assess the general applicability of the proposed method


-  While the proposed criterion is meant to be used in internal validation, at the end the evaluation is based on external measures, i.e. accuracy and ARI. Of course it is a somehow standard and well established way, still it would be nice at least to discuss alternatives and (possibly) provide examples – like, for example, evaluation based on context knowledge, in the spirit of what is discussed in papers like: 
Ulrike von Luxburg, Robert C. Williamson, Isabelle Guyon: Clustering: Science or Art? ICML Unsupervised and Transfer Learning 2012: 65-80
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written. One comment: authors qualitatively justify their approach using fig 1. I think that clusters of figure 1(b) are definitely not realistic: it is very rare that a clustering algorithm, given the data represented in figure, would output such clusters.

For what concerns novelty, maybe authors should refer and compare to other works in clustering evaluation which make use of Information theoretic concepts, like for example the (somehow old but just to give an idea):
Vinh, Epps, Bailey: Information Theoretic Measures for Clusterings Comparison: Variants, Properties, Normalization and Correction for Chance 
Journal of Machine Learning Research 11 (2010) 2837-2854
content.summary_of_the_review:
Somehow interesting paper dealing with a crucial problem. The approach can be better contextualized, some assumptions (like Gaussianity of Clusters) are rather strong, and better alternatives exists.

UPDATE AFTER REBUTTAL
I carefully read the responses, the clarifications, and the additional material, and I thank the authors for the significant efforts made in clarifying my doubts. Even if I consider that the paper has potential, I’ll maintain my score unchanged, since I still have some doubts, especially on the assumptions: even if I acknowledge the efforts made by the authors in improving this aspect in the rebuttal, I still consider that the Gaussianity assumption is rather strong, and that better alternatives exist.
------

Details can be seen in Appendix E, and based on the aforementioned analysis, deep representation is beneficial for our IP index. The size of the embedding is reported in Appendix C, and following previous deep learning works, we also use the default embedding size returned by different deep models, i.e., BERT, SBERT, SimCSE, ViT and BEiT return 768 embedding size and Swin returns 1024 embedding size. 
Moreover, most existing deep clustering works [1][2][3][4][5][6][7] focus on leaning better data representations and the most widely used baseline in these works is to first use contrastive learning to learn good representation and then use KMeans to obtain clustering result. Experimental results show that this baseline outperforms many deep clustering methods. Considering that our work is not to study clustering algorithm, we also follow the baseline tradition for our work.   
  Among the clustering methods we used, Dbscan can return non-convex clusters and experimental results in our paper show that our IP index is not sensitive to non-convex clusters and can also reliably evaluate the clustering results.  
[1] Van Gansbeke W, Vandenhende S, Georgoulis S, et al. Scan: Learning to classify images without labels[C]// ECCV 2020.  
[2] Huang S, Wei F, Cui L, et al. Unsupervised fine-tuning for text clustering[C]//COLING 2020.  
[3]Tsai T W, Li C, Zhu J. Mice: Mixture of contrastive experts for unsupervised image clustering[C]//ICLR 2020.  
[4] Zhang D, Nan F, Wei X, et al. Supporting clustering with contrastive learning[J]. NAACL2021.  
[5] Shen Y, Shen Z, Wang M, et al. You never cluster alone[J]. NIPS 2021.  
[6] Dang Z, Deng C, Yang X, et al. Nearest neighbor matching for deep clustering[C]//CVPR 2021.  
[7] Li Y, Hu P, Liu Z, et al. Contrastive clustering[C]// AAAI 2021.  

**Response 1.3:**  As far as we know, existing works all use external indices to evaluate the clustering results. Moreover, evaluation based on context knowledge usually depend on the current particular application, such as recommender system. To the best of our knowledge, there are currently no datasets that support us to complete such experiment.

**Response 1.4:** For the clusters of figure 1(b), we just use a simple 2D example to show that variance- based compactness computation fail to provide a reliable validation when two clusters have the same variance. In fact, it may produce such clusters in a 3D space or higher dimensional space.

**Response 1.5:** In the revision, we have added the experiments of normalized mutual information (NMI) in Section 5.2. NMI makes use of information theoretic concepts for evaluating clustering results. Our proposed method still outperforms other indices significantly.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposed an internal validation index for clustering based on differential entropy, which is calculated by using a gaussianity  assumption. 

All reviewers agree that the paper should not be published. Most reviewers believe that the gaussianity assumption is too strong, and that the paper makes limited contributions to the field.
